newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic group victorious after post-war election.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic group victorious after post-war election.

text.p: Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition held a convincing lead on Tuesday after Yugoslavia's first post-war elections in which the Serbian president stressed his role as peacemaker.

The federal election commmission said by Monday evening Milosevic's coalition had secured 50 seats, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition 21 and ultra-nationalist Radicals 13, according to initial results of Sunday's poll.
Party officials said Milosevic's coalition was on the way to securing a clear majority in the federal parliament of Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro.

The hard-fought election campaign of the leftist coalition, comprising Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS), the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), led by his powerful wife Mirjana Markovic, and New Democracy, paid off handsomely, diplomats said.

It managed to obliterate the bitter memories of the dead and deprivation from the four-year war in the Balkans mainly due to its message of peace, tolerance, religious and racial equality and rapprochement among peoples, they said.
Aleksandar Vulin, spokesman for JUL, said the coalition had "for sure" two-thirds of 108 seats allocated to Serbia in the federal parliament.
Together with the seats won by the allied Montenegrin Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), the results promised Milosevic total control over the federal parliament.
In Montenegro, the DPS proclaimed victory in the republic's parliamentary elections, which coincided with the federal and municipal polls, winning 45 seats in the 71-member parliament.
Diplomats say Milosevic will probably assume the post of federal president after the next parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.
Milosevic has frequently told his people after he helped engineer the Dayton peace accord last November it was time to turn to the future, work and prosperity.
"It was music to the ears of many people in Serbia, who were sick and tired of the war they obviously never really believed in anyway," a Western diplomat said.
One-third of the 10.5 million population is living in poverty, according to a recent Red Cross survey.
The opposition tried to capitalise on the issue, saying Milosevic was leading the people into yet greater misery.

It promised speedy privatisation, along the lines set by popular former central bank governor Dragoslav Avramovic, who managed to unite the opposition and briefly lead it before stepping down for reasons that remain unclear.
But its message did not get across mainly due to the tight grip by Milosevic's parties over state television -- the most important medium in a country where most are too poor to buy newspapers.
Opposition parties, covering the political spectrum from liberal to right-wing nationalist, privately acknowledged defeat.

Opposition officials blamed the state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians which gave the left coalition 15 seats on a platter, lack of interest by the West and voter apathy for their poor performance.
"If anything, Milosevic knows how to rule. I just could not stand more hyperinflation, sanctions or a new war," one 28-year old computer expert said.
